alignment.note: Greek περιεβλέπετο is a single imperfect middle verb conveying durative aspect; Syriac renders this periphrastically with ܘܚܐܪ ('and he looked') plus the auxiliary ܗܘܐ ('was'), a characteristic Syriac construction for past continuous action. Latin circumspiciebat captures the same durative imperfect in a single inflected form.

Greek uses a single articular substantival participle construction (τὴν … ποιήσασαν, 'the [woman] who had done'); Syriac employs an interrogative-relative ܡܢܘ ('who [it was that]'), while Latin splits the head into a pronoun plus relative (eam, quæ), each tradition realising the substantival relative differently.

Greek ποιήσασαν is a feminine accusative aorist participle agreeing with the article and explicitly marking the female agent; Syriac ܥܒܕ is a finite verb within the relative clause governed by ܡܢܘ, and Latin fecerat is a pluperfect finite verb in the relative clause — three distinct syntactic strategies for the same predication.
